opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it changed my understanding quite a lot. Before I started the company, I came mostly from a research background, and I think I had a fairly naive picture of fundraising. I imagined it as something like a paper review: you present your technical work, people evaluate whether it's good, and if it's strong enough, you get funded. Going through it myself, I realized it's a very different kind of process.

First, investors aren't really evaluating the technology alone; they're evaluating a story about the future and whether *you* are the team that can make that future happen. The technical depth matters a lot, especially in AI infrastructure, but it's the entry ticket, not the whole conversation. What they really want to understand is: why now, why this team, and how big this can get if things go right. I had to learn to translate what I knew deeply as a researcher into language about markets, timing, and leverage.

Second, I learned that fundraising is very much a two-way selection. Early on, you feel like you're the one being judged. But over time I realized I was also choosing partners who would be around the table for many years. Some investors ask very sharp questions that actually help you think more clearly about your own business; others are just pattern-matching. The good ones push you without trying to steer you away from what you believe in. That became a big part of how I decided who to work with.

Third, I came to see that conviction is contagious, both ways. When I was clear about why our approach mattered, the conversations went better. When I was hedging, people could feel it immediately. So fundraising actually forced me to sharpen my own thinking about what we're building and what we're not building.

And finally, I think I became much more calm about rejection. In research, a rejected paper can feel very personal. In fundraising, a "no" often just means it's not the right fit for that fund's thesis or timing. Once I internalized that, I stopped trying to convince everyone and focused on finding the people who genuinely shared the vision. That shift made the whole process healthier, for me and for the company.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, before I started raising, I had a pretty naive picture of fundraising. I thought of it almost like a research grant review: you write up what you're doing, the evaluators look at the technical merit, and the best idea wins. Coming from a systems and infrastructure background, I assumed the pitch was mostly about the technology.

What I learned very quickly is that investors are not evaluating your technology in isolation. They're evaluating a story about the future, and whether you are the right person to make that future happen. A lot of the conversations that went well had surprisingly little to do with the details of our architecture. They were about why now, why this market, why this team, and what happens if it works. The technical depth matters, but it mostly serves as proof that you can execute, not as the thing being bought.

The second shift was understanding that investors are people with their own constraints. A fund has a thesis, a stage they invest at, a check size, and partners who have to defend the deal internally. Early on I took every "no" personally, like it was a verdict on the idea. Later I realized many of those were really "not for us," or "not at this stage," or "we already have something adjacent in the portfolio." Once I understood that, I started treating fundraising more like a matching problem. Who is actually set up to say yes to a company like ours? That saved a lot of time and emotional energy.

The third thing, and maybe the most important, is that the best investors were the ones who pushed back hardest in the meeting. They would poke at the go-to-market, ask who the first ten customers really are, question whether open source was a moat or a liability. Those conversations were uncomfortable, but they sharpened our thinking far more than the friendly ones. So now I look at fundraising less as asking for money and more as a very intense form of customer discovery for the business itself.

And finally, it changed how I think about leverage. When you have real traction, whether that's usage, a community, or a few paying customers, the dynamic flips completely. The same investor who was lukewarm six months earlier suddenly wants to move quickly. So my advice to other technical founders is: raise when you have something concrete to show, know what each investor actually needs, and treat the hard questions as a gift rather than an attack.

astra-6.text:
Raising money has made me realize that fundraising is less about convincing everyone that your idea is good and more about finding the investors whose interests and expectations match what you’re building. You can have the same conversation with two investors and get completely different reactions. That doesn’t necessarily mean one understands the business and the other doesn’t—they may have different views on timing, market size, or the kind of risk they’re willing to take.

It’s also changed how I think about rejection. My instinct was to treat every no as feedback on the company. Now I try to distinguish between a concern we really need to address and a mismatch that a better pitch won’t solve. You want to listen carefully without constantly changing direction to satisfy whoever you spoke to most recently.

And I think much more about the relationship after the investment. Getting a check is one moment. You’re going to be working with that person through uncertainty, and you need to be able to have honest conversations when things aren’t going well. So fundraising is also a chance for you to understand the investor: how they think, what they expect, and whether you can build that trust.

sol-6.1.text:
Raising money has made me see fundraising as a two-way evaluation. You’re trying to help investors understand your company, but you’re also figuring out whether they’re the right partners for you.

I’ve also learned that a rejection isn’t necessarily a judgment on the business. Investors have different priorities, different levels of conviction, and different constraints. You have to listen carefully to the feedback without letting every conversation change your direction.

For me, the biggest shift is understanding that getting the money is only the beginning. You’re choosing people you’ll work with through uncertainty, so how they think and how they communicate matter a lot.
